title: Matrices, Lists and Data Frames
subtitle: Matrices, lists, factors and data frames for structured data.
description: Master the main data structures used in R and learn how to organize information for analysis.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand Matrices, Lists and Data Frames

Welcome to Lesson 5: Matrices, Lists and Data Frames. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Matrices, Lists and Data Frames”. The goal is to matrices, lists, factors and data frames for structured data.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
R offers vectors, matrices, lists, factors, and data frames for different shapes of information. A data frame aligns columns of equal length, and each column can represent a different variable.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.question: What makes a final coding project reproducible?
options: A screenshot of a successful run only.
A single unexplained binary.
Source, clear run instructions, and testable expected behavior.
A note saying “works on my phone.”
blocks.explanation: Source and repeatable instructions let another person verify the behavior independently.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.

blocks.question: A final application calculates correct totals for typical inputs. What else should be tested before release?
options: Only the title font.
Only the happy path.
Invalid, empty, boundary, and error cases as well as normal input.
Nothing, because the examples ran once.
blocks.explanation: Boundary and failure-path testing catches common defects that a happy-path run misses.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.

blocks.text: Choose a structure based on how data will be accessed and transformed. A list can contain mixed objects; a matrix is rectangular and typically uses one atomic type.

blocks.question: A project repeats the same validation rule in four places and the rules now disagree. What should be done?
options: Centralize the rule in a reusable function and test it.
Add a fifth copy.
Remove the validation everywhere.
Make the rule depend on screen size.
blocks.explanation: A single tested rule avoids inconsistent copies and reduces maintenance cost.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A single tested rule avoids inconsistent copies and reduces maintenance cost.

blocks.question: A project’s output looks correct but the code is difficult to maintain. What is the best next step?
options: Rename every variable randomly.
Add a second implementation without removing the first.
Ignore structure because the output is right.
Separate responsibilities, improve names, and add targeted tests.
blocks.explanation: Maintainability and tests make later changes safer, beyond simply matching one output.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Maintainability and tests make later changes safer, beyond simply matching one output.

blocks.question: An application relies on a service that may be unavailable. Which state should the UI or CLI handle?
options: Success only.
A clear loading/success/error or recovery state.
No output until it crashes.
A fabricated result.
blocks.explanation: Real applications must communicate expected failure states and avoid claiming work succeeded when it did not.
